assets.statement: f(1+p+q)=pq refuted: n=15=1+3+11 has f(15)=8 (m=8: 1+2+4+8)<33 and n=25=1+11+13 has f(25)=36 (m=36: 1+2+3+4+6+9)<143; the canonical witness is not the minimizer, so balanced Goldbach yields only an upper bound and cannot close part (iii).

Parity lemma refuted by Kummer: k&(n−k)=0 gives odd C(n,k); (7,3)=35 with lpf 5>7/2, and infinitely many (2^m−1,k) instances; branch-A close must instead bound small prime factors of odd coefficients directly.
witness (n,k)=(7,3): C(7,3)=35, lpf=5 > max(7/3,3)=3, refuting the strict ∀-form; canonical statement survives only via its finitely-many-exceptions clause, so branch B cannot close on L1 alone.
Finite-prime covering is impossible (uncovered periodic class of positive density), so any affirmative construction must use infinitely many primes — a provable obstruction, not a resolution.

L1 proves only monotonicity/collision-persistence and per-pair semi-decision; it covers no instance of the required ∀m,n ∃i,j coverage, so it cannot close branch A (and no counterexample supports branch B).

refuted at smallest parameters: r=2, k=2 family I₁={2,3}, I₂={24,25} gives total product 3600=60², exactly verified; Pell a(a+1)=6t² yields infinitely many length-2 square-product blocks, so k=2 imposes no obstruction and any close must use a fixed r across all k≥2 with explicit integrality.
